opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think these are two pretty different things, and the interesting part is how they interact.

When I'm doing security work, a lot of the time the first signal is just a feeling. You look at a defense or a paper's evaluation and something doesn't sit right. The numbers are too clean, or the robustness curve is suspiciously flat, or the defense works against every attack equally well. I usually can't say why at first. It's pattern matching from having seen a lot of broken things before.

That feeling isn't evidence on its own. Plenty of times I've thought "this has to be broken" and it turned out to be fine. So the explicit reasoning is what you do next: you write down what the defense is supposed to do, you ask what an adaptive attacker would try, and you go and try it. The intuition tells you where to look. The reasoning tells you whether you were right.

I think the same structure applies to whether you're being tricked more generally, for people or for models. The intuitive alarm is cheap and fast and catches a lot. But it's also exactly what a good adversary is optimizing against. If someone is trying to fool you, they make the thing feel normal. The most dangerous attacks are the ones that don't set off the alarm. So you can't rely only on "does this feel off." Sometimes you need a deliberate procedure that you run even when everything feels fine.

The other direction matters too. Explicit reasoning can talk you out of a correct intuition. You build a nice argument for why something is safe, it's internally consistent, and you override the part of you that said "wait." Attackers can exploit that as well, by giving you a plausible story. So I'd say the healthy version treats the gut feeling as a reason to slow down and check carefully, not as a verdict, and never lets a clever argument fully overrule that feeling until you've actually tested it.

For language models, I think a lot of what we call jailbreak resistance is really this intuitive layer: the model has learned that certain inputs look like manipulation. That's useful, but it's brittle in the same way human intuition is, because you can dress the attack up so it doesn't look like one. Whether models can do the slower, explicit "am I being manipulated here, and how would I tell?" reasoning reliably, and whether that's actually more robust, is one of the more interesting open questions to me right now.

r001.rationale: The response says the intuitive alarm tells you where to look and prompts deliberate checking, while explicit reasoning determines whether the suspicion was right.

r002.rationale: It describes the feeling as pattern matching from prior experience, but does not suggest it arises from recursive internal thinking before conscious, verbal reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because a big part of what I do is basically trying to trick things. When you're attacking a system, you're looking for the gap between what the thing actually does and what it thinks it's doing, or what the designer thinks it's doing. And the interesting thing is that the defense against that often starts as a feeling before it's an argument.

So, concretely, I'd say the intuition is usually right that something is wrong, and usually wrong about what. When I'm reading a paper and I get that little itch, "hm, that number is too clean," or "why did they pick that baseline," I've learned to trust that the itch is pointing at something. But if I just stop there and say "this feels off," that's not useful. I can't publish that, and honestly I can't even act on it reliably, because the feeling is just as easily produced by a paper being written in a style I don't like.

The way I'd put it is, the intuition is a cheap detector with a high false positive rate, and the explicit reasoning is the expensive verifier. The intuition's job is to decide where to spend the expensive thing. And the failure mode in both directions is pretty clear. If you only have the intuition, you end up with people who are suspicious of everything and can't tell you why, and they get fooled anyway, just by different tricks. If you only have the explicit reasoning, you never even start the investigation, because you never noticed there was anything to check. Most of the adversarial examples work, most of the data extraction stuff, started with "wait, that shouldn't be possible," and then months of actually making it work.

The other thing I'd say is the explicit reasoning trains the intuition. Every time you sit down and actually work out why something was wrong, the next time you see that pattern, you don't have to do the work again. It just feels off. So people who look like they have great instincts about when they're being tricked, I think, mostly just have a lot of cached explicit reasoning. And the inverse is true too, which is sort of uncomfortable. If you're in a domain where you've never done the careful version, your "something is off" feeling is basically noise, and you should probably weight it accordingly.

And this matters for how I think about models, too. When someone says a model "senses" that a prompt is manipulative, I want to know whether that's a learned shortcut that happens to correlate with manipulation, or whether there's any verification happening. Because the shortcut is exactly what an attacker optimizes against. The feeling is the first thing to break. So I'd say, trust the feeling enough to go look, and never trust it enough to stop looking.

r001.rationale: The response calls intuition a “cheap detector” that directs where to spend explicit reasoning, described as an “expensive verifier.”

r002.rationale: The response says prior explicit reasoning can train intuition, but does not say the initial feeling arises from recursive internal thinking before conscious, verbal reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think the intuition often comes first, and then the explicit reasoning is an attempt to figure out what triggered it. You see something and think, “Wait, that’s weird.” You might not yet be able to say whether it’s a contradiction, an unusual request, or something that doesn’t fit the context. But it gives you a reason to stop and look more carefully.

The tricky part is that these aren’t necessarily independent checks. If I have a feeling that something is wrong and then ask myself to explain why, I can come up with a plausible explanation that isn’t actually correct. So the useful question is less “Can I justify this feeling?” and more “What evidence would distinguish someone trying to trick me from an innocent explanation?”

I’d treat the intuition as a signal to investigate. The explicit reasoning is useful when it turns that signal into something you can check.

r001.rationale: The response describes intuition as an initial signal to stop and investigate, with explicit reasoning used to assess whether someone is trying to trick you.

r002.rationale: It says the intuition may come before you can explain it, but does not say it arises from recursive internal thinking before conscious verbal reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the intuitive feeling often comes first, and the explicit reasoning is your attempt to figure out what triggered it. You notice something that doesn’t quite fit, but you can’t necessarily articulate why. Then you stop and ask, “Okay, what would have to be true for this to make sense? And what would it look like if someone were trying to trick me?”

But those aren’t independent checks. If your reasoning is just finding a story to justify your initial feeling, you haven’t really gained much. The useful step is to identify something you can actually test—some evidence that would distinguish an innocent explanation from a deceptive one. So I’d treat that feeling as a reason to investigate, rather than as evidence that you’ve already figured it out.

r001.rationale: The response says the intuitive feeling often comes first and prompts explicit reasoning to identify what triggered it, including whether someone might be trying to trick you.

r002.rationale: It says the feeling can precede conscious reasoning, but does not suggest that recursive internal thinking produces the feeling.
